wine.name: Schloss Johannisberger Riesling Grünlack Spätlese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Spätlese: late picked, at least 85 degrees Oechsle in the Rheingau
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, as the hill has been planted since 1720.
wine.sites: The estate's single vineyard in one piece on the hill below the schloss, above the Rhine: Taunus quartzite under fertile loam and loess, with a little iron oxide that tints the soil red.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel, by the estate's own sheets, and kept on its fine lees until bottling in the spring after the harvest. The fermentation ends with a clear natural sweetness left in the wine and a low alcohol, well under ten per cent.
wine.glass: Ripe apple, white peach and quince over orange zest and wet stone; a clear sweetness held by firm Rheingau acidity, with age bringing honey, toast and smoke.
wine.ageing: Pleasing young, it gains depth for ten to twenty years, and a strong vintage lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The green capsule of the estate's colour code, marking its Spätlese.
The estate's own name, a district of Geisenheim allowed on the label with no village before it.
Late picked, at least 85 degrees Oechsle in the Rheingau; the word the estate's legend of 1775 gave the language.

records.table: A green capsule marks Schloss Johannisberg's Grünlack Spätlese, Riesling from the hill where, as the estate tells it, the late harvest of 1775 gave Germany the word. Apple and peach over stone, it is plainly sweet with a firm backbone.
records.story: The estate counts twelve centuries of wine on its hill, and around 1100 Benedictine monks founded a monastery there. By 1716, when the Prince-Abbot of Fulda bought it, the monastery lay in ruins; Fulda built a summer palace and from 1720 planted the hill to Riesling alone. In 1775, so the story goes, the courier sent to Fulda for the Prince-Abbot's leave to pick came back late; the grapes had shrivelled and caught noble rot, the wine made from them was a revelation, and Spätlese, the late harvest, entered the language. The estate's chronology adds its first Eiswein in 1858. On 1 July 1816, after the Congress of Vienna, the Emperor Francis I of Austria (1768 to 1835) gave the schloss to his foreign minister, Prince Klemens von Metternich (1773 to 1859), with a tithe of the yield owed each year to the Habsburgs. By its own account its cellar library holds bottles back to 1748. The estate came to code its wines by the colour of the capsule, the Rotlack for Kabinett, the Grünlack for Spätlese and the Silberlack for its dry Grosses Gewächs, so a guest can read the style from across the room. The Grünlack carries the legend into the glass; tell it as the estate's claim rather than as proven history.

wine.name: Kiedrich Gräfenberg Riesling Trockenbeerenauslese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Trockenbeerenauslese: shrivelled noble rot berries, at least 150 degrees Oechsle
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from berries shrivelled by noble rot.
wine.sites: The Gräfenberg, a steep slope above Kiedrich facing south south west, with gradients up to 60 per cent on deep, stony soils of phyllite mixed with loess.
wine.making: Pickers go through the vineyard again and again, taking shrivelled, noble rot berries one by one. The thick, sticky juice ferments slowly to a low alcohol, well under ten per cent, with a great weight of natural sugar left behind.
wine.glass: Dried apricot, candied orange peel and saffron over acacia honey and caramelised pineapple; syrupy yet electric, its intense sweetness carried by high acidity to a finish that seems to last for minutes.
wine.ageing: Already rich on release, it lives for half a century and more, slowly turning towards toffee, black tea and dried fig.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a small pour, alone or with a fruit tart.

label.means: The village and the vineyard; older labels read Kiedricher Gräfenberg.
Dried berry selection: shrivelled noble rot berries picked one by one, at least 150 degrees Oechsle.
The region on the Rhine's north bank between Wiesbaden and Rüdesheim.

records.table: Single shrivelled berries, picked one by one on the steep slate of the Gräfenberg above Kiedrich, make Robert Weil's Riesling Trockenbeerenauslese. Honeyed and syrupy, apricot and orange peel, yet bright with acidity, it is a dessert served in a small glass.
records.story: The estate began with a scholar. Its founder, a German professor at the Sorbonne in Paris, bought his first vines on the Kiedricher Berg in 1867, by the estate's account, and the events before the war of 1870 drove him out of France. In 1875, the year the house counts as its founding, he added more of the Kiedrich slope, and he bought the manor house of a late English baronet in the village, which became the seat of the estate. As the house tells it, its Spätlese and Auslese wines were poured at imperial and royal courts across Europe. In 1988 the Japanese house of Suntory took a majority of the estate, with the founder's great grandson, the fourth generation, in charge of the wine. By the estate's own account the Gräfenberg has given every Prädikat up to Trockenbeerenauslese in every vintage since 1989, while the same slope gives a dry Grosses Gewächs. That run made Weil the usual counterweight to the Mosel when a question asks for German sweet Riesling. Against a Saar Trockenbeerenauslese the Rheingau's way with noble rot is plain to taste: the same grape in a fuller, firmer frame.

wine.name: Schloss Vollrads Riesling Kabinett
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Kabinett: the ripeness level below Spätlese; a VDP village wine on the estate's labels
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, the grape of almost the whole estate.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyards at Winkel, its own monopole around the moated tower above the village among them, on loess over Taunus quartzite, between the Rhine and the Taunus.
wine.making: The Kabinett is made in two styles: off dry, labelled feinherb, and fruity, plainly sweet at a low alcohol. By the estate's own sheet the feinherb is raised wholly in stainless steel; the estate's dry village wine is bottled apart, as 1716 Cabinet.
wine.glass: Green apple, lemon zest and white peach over wet stone, with a hint of fresh mint; light, crisp and restrained, the sweetness of each style balanced by firm acidity.
wine.ageing: Fresh and easy young, it keeps and gains for ten years and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with river fish, asparagus or a light salad.

label.means: The estate, an Ortsteil of Winkel; on its dry 1716 Cabinet the name stands alone, with no village.
The village, printed on the Kabinett as a VDP village wine in the estate's labels since at least 2020.
The Prädikat below Spätlese; the estate makes it off dry or fruity and sweet.

records.table: Schloss Vollrads, above Winkel, dates its sales of wine to 1211 by its own account. Its Riesling Kabinett, from loess over quartzite, comes off dry, labelled feinherb, or fruity and sweet: light and crisp, green apple and lemon over stone.
records.story: In 1211 the Greiffenclau family appear at Winkel in the service of the Archbishop of Mainz, and a sale of wine recorded that year is where Schloss Vollrads begins its own history. From about 1330 the family lived in the moated tower at the heart of the estate, for more than three hundred and fifty years, until they built the manor house beside it in 1684. The name passed in time to the Matuschka-Greiffenclau line. Erwein Graf Matuschka-Greiffenclau (1938 to 1997), who took over the indebted estate in 1975, was among the founders in 1984 of Charta, the growers' association that set out to bring dry Rheingau Riesling back to the table; its vineyards joined the VDP in 1999, the year the Rheingau's Erstes Gewächs arrived. His death in 1997 ended nearly eight centuries of the family at Vollrads, and the estate passed to a regional savings bank, the Nassauische Sparkasse, which kept its name and its Riesling. The Kabinett is the estate's everyday voice and the plainest sign of its long habit of making one wine in more than one style. Its label is the lesson: read feinherb, or its absence, before you pour.

wine.name: Rüdesheim Berg Schlossberg Riesling
wine.sites: The Berg Schlossberg, the steep castle hill of the Rüdesheimer Berg at the Rhine's bend, facing south south west on Taunus quartzite and phyllite slate, a soil that drains freely and stores the heat.
wine.making: Fermented and raised for most of a year in old oak casks of the Rheingau's traditional sizes, then bottled dry. The wine is labelled by village and vineyard alone, with no Prädikat.
wine.glass: Smoke, struck flint and wet slate over lime, yellow apple and blood orange; taut and bone dry, firm in grip and long, with a stony, faintly bitter edge at the finish.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first five to eight years, it then opens and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The castle hill of the Rüdesheimer Berg, the steep slope at the Rhine's bend.
The village, written before the vineyard; older labels read Rüdesheimer.
The grape; no Prädikat follows, since the estate labels by site alone and the wine is dry.

records.table: Georg Breuer labels its Rüdesheim Berg Schlossberg Riesling by place alone, with no Prädikat, the estate's way with its dry wines. Grown on steep quartzite and slate at the Rhine's bend and raised in old casks, it is bone dry, smoky and taut.
records.story: Dry Riesling named for its vineyard is the idea that made the Breuer name. The estate grew from a Rüdesheim wine business founded in 1880, which a partner from the Breuer family took over early in the twentieth century, and it carries the name of a later head of the family. In the 1980s his son led it towards one idea: that Rheingau Riesling should be dry, and should be named for the vineyard it came from rather than for its ripeness at harvest. In 1984 he was among the founders of Charta, the growers' association that set a standard for dry Rheingau Riesling from good sites. The estate went further and dropped the Prädikat words from its labels altogether, naming its wines by village and vineyard alone. The Rheingau's Erstes Gewächs followed in 1999, when Charta's vineyards joined the VDP, and with the 2012 vintage the VDP's Rheingau members moved to Grosses Gewächs. He died suddenly in May 2004, aged 57, and his daughter took over the estate young and kept its course. The Berg Schlossberg, the steep quartzite and slate of the castle hill above the river, is the summit of the range. A place on the label and nothing else was the argument, and no wine of the estate makes it louder than the Berg Schlossberg.

report: Rechecked with six searches of its own and two shared with the group on 12 November 2026; the estate's own pages were not reached, so the record rests on the VDP's vineyard and regional pages (primary) and on two secondary sources for each fact, listed in reviews/recheck-rheingau.json.

Corrected: the estate grew from a Rüdesheim wine business of 1880 that a Breuer partner took over early in the twentieth century, by an importer and a wine guide, not a family at Rüdesheim since the late nineteenth century; founded stays empty, since 1880 is the business's year and not the family's.
Corrected: the Berg Schlossberg faces south south west on Taunus quartzite and phyllite slate by the VDP; the terraces walled in stone, found in no source, are taken out.

Corrected: the wine ferments and rests for some eight to eleven months in old oak casks by three merchants' sheets; the library's spontaneous fermentation is contested by one importer's cultured yeasts, so the yeast is left out and reported.
Corrected: Erstes Gewächs arrived with the Charta vineyards' entry to the VDP in 1999 by the VDP and the Hessian soil survey; the question no longer says the state wrote it into law.
The son who led the estate died in May 2004 aged 57 by Decanter and an importer, but his birth year is in one source only, so he stays described; the daughter is living and not named.
Left out: the artist labels said to date from 1980 (one importer only), the ruined castle that names the hill, and the estate leaving the VDP, which one wine guide implies.

story: a Rüdesheim wine business of 1880 taken over early in the twentieth century by a Breuer partner, in place of the family at Rüdesheim since the late nineteenth century; the son among Charta's founders in 1984; Erstes Gewächs with the Charta vineyards in 1999 rather than written into law by Hesse; his sudden death in May 2004 aged 57.

wine.name: Steinberger Riesling
wine.classification: An Ortsteil: the walled vineyard registered with the standing of a village
wine.sites: The Steinberg, the walled vineyard some 900 metres from the abbey above Hattenheim, a monopole of the state domaine on a slope facing south to south west: sandy loess and loam below, stony slate and quartzite higher up.
wine.making: Made since 2008 in the Steinbergkeller, the cellar the state domaine opened beside the vineyard. The Steinberger is bottled dry and in the Prädikat styles, and a Wild Ferment cuvée ferments on the vineyard's own wild yeasts; the dry Grosses Gewächs is labelled Steinberg alone.
wine.glass: Yellow apple, quince and lemon peel over smoke and wet stone; dry, firm and broad in the Rheingau way, with a long, faintly salty finish.
wine.ageing: Firm young, it opens after three to five years and keeps for fifteen years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a white wine glass.

label.means: Wine of the Steinberg, registered in 1971 as a part of Hattenheim and labelled without a village name.
The Cistercian abbey of 1136, whose name the state wine domaine carries.
Dry, the style of the domaine's everyday Steinberger.

records.table: Planted by the Cistercians of Kloster Eberbach and walled by them in the eighteenth century, the Steinberg above Hattenheim gives Steinberger Riesling. Made dry, it is broad and firm, yellow apple and quince over smoke and stone.
records.story: An earlier religious house in the wooded valley above Hattenheim had failed when, in 1136, twelve monks came from Clairvaux, the abbey of Bernard of Clairvaux (1090 to 1153), at the request of the Archbishop of Mainz and founded the Cistercian abbey of Eberbach. Their Steinberg, on the slope below the forest, appears by name in the abbey's register of goods in 1211, and in the eighteenth century the monks closed it with a stone wall, finished in 1767. By most accounts the word Cabinet was first written at Eberbach in 1712, for reserve wines the monks set apart in a cellar of their own, and as Kabinett it later came to name a Prädikat. When the abbey was dissolved in 1803 it became the princely wine cellar of the Dukes of Nassau; after Nassau lost the war of 1866 it was a royal Prussian domaine, and after the Second World War it passed to the new state of Hesse, whose state wine domaine made the abbey and the Steinberg its home. The wine law of 1971 registered the Steinberg as a part of Hattenheim, so its wine is labelled Steinberger, with no village name. One wall, one vineyard, one name: eight centuries of monks, dukes, kings and a state stand behind the label.

traps: Steinberg is a vineyard, not a village; Steinberger on a label is an Ortsteil of Hattenheim.
Kloster Eberbach is the Cistercians' abbey and the state wine domaine; Schloss Johannisberg was the Benedictines' hill.
The Steinberg's wall is a work of the eighteenth century, finished in 1767, not of the Middle Ages, though the vineyard is named in 1211.

cards.front: Kloster Eberbach: what was the Cabinet of 1712, and what word did it give?
cards.back: Reserve wines the monks set apart in a cellar of their own; it gave the Prädikat Kabinett its name.

cards.front: Steinberger Riesling: who planted the Steinberg, and when was its wall finished?
cards.back: The Cistercian monks of Kloster Eberbach; they closed it with a stone wall in the eighteenth century, finished in 1767.

questions.q: A guest reads Steinberger on a Kloster Eberbach Riesling and asks which village that is. What do you say?
opts: None: it is the abbey's walled vineyard, an Ortsteil
A village beside Rüdesheim at the Rhine's bend
A Grosslage covering the slopes of Hattenheim
A district name for the whole Rheingau
questions.exp: The Steinberg is the Cistercians' walled vineyard above Hattenheim, registered in 1971 with village standing as an Ortsteil; the whole Rheingau as one district is Bereich Johannisberg.

questions.q: Which order of monks came to Eberbach in 1136, founded its abbey and planted the vineyard that became the walled Steinberg?
opts: The Cistercians
The Benedictines
The Augustinians
The Carthusians
questions.exp: Twelve Cistercian monks from Clairvaux founded Eberbach in 1136, after an earlier house there had failed; the Benedictines held the hill at Johannisberg.

report: The house is not in the library. Rechecked with nine searches of its own and one shared with the group on 12 November 2026; the domaine's own history, Steinberg and abbey pages on kloster-eberbach.de were read through search summaries, listed in reviews/recheck-rheingau.json.

Corrected: the wall was built in the eighteenth century and finished in 1767, by the domaine and Wikipedia (an importer's sheet agrees on the century), so the table no longer says the Cistercians walled it in the Middle Ages.
Corrected: the Steinberg is named in the abbey's register of 1211; its laying out in the twelfth century, around 1170 in one account, is left unstated.
Corrected: Clairvaux sent twelve monks at the Archbishop of Mainz's request to a site where an earlier house had failed, by the abbey's own page; Bernard's dates 1090 to 1153 come from the same page.

Added with sources: the domaine's Steinbergkeller of 2008, the soils of sandy loess and loam with stony slate and quartzite, the south to south west slope, the Ortsteil registered in 1971, and the line 1803, 1866 and after 1945 by the domaine's own history.

Taken out: wine shipped down the Rhine to Cologne, steel in the cellar and a fermentation called cool, none of them found; the Höllenberg red and the Steinberger Auslese give way to the Grosses Gewächs, the Crescentia and the Wild Ferment, which the domaine's own pages name.

The pick: the domaine's dry top wine is labelled Steinberg Grosses Gewächs and its Steinberger Riesling trocken sits at the VDP village level; the record keeps the plan's Steinberger Riesling and teaches the difference.

changed: classification and label[0]: the Steinberg registered with village standing as a part of Hattenheim by the wine law of 1971, by a wine encyclopedia and Wikipedia; a third label term, trocken.

sites: some 900 metres from the abbey, a monopole facing south to south west, sandy loess and loam below with stony slate and quartzite higher up, by the domaine and an importer's sheet, where it said a gentle south facing hill.

making: the Steinbergkeller of 2008 by the domaine, the Steinberger dry and in the Prädikat styles, the Wild Ferment on the vineyard's own yeasts and the Grosses Gewächs labelled Steinberg alone; the cool ferment in steel and the old vintages in the Cabinet cellar are cut, found nowhere.
table: walled in the eighteenth century, not in the Middle Ages.

story: twelve monks from Clairvaux at the Archbishop of Mainz's request where an earlier house had failed, by the abbey's own page; the Steinberg named in the abbey's register of 1211; the wall finished in 1767; the Cabinet of 1712 as reserve wines in a cellar of their own, by most accounts; 1803 Nassau, 1866 Prussia, after the war Hesse, by the domaine's history; the 1971 registration; the wine to Cologne cut.

others, traps and cards: the Grosses Gewächs, the Crescentia and the Wild Ferment from the domaine's pages in place of the Höllenberg red and the Auslese; a trap on the wall of the eighteenth century in place of the Cabinet trap; the card asks when the wall was finished.
questions[1]: the monks who came to Eberbach in 1136, with the Augustinians as a distractor in place of the Capuchins, whose planting of Weinbach's clos the Alsace recheck no longer holds.
sources: five pages a search returned, three the domaine's own, in place of the Codex's own records and an unopened book.
story: the close names monks, dukes, kings and a state, since the abbey was secular from 1803 and eight centuries of monastic history was too long.
open: Whether the earlier house at Eberbach was of Augustinian canons from 1116, in one source only; the record says only that it had failed.
The year the Steinberg was first planted: around 1170 in one source; the record says only that it is named in 1211.
The Steinberg as an Ortsteil rests on a wine encyclopedia and Wikipedia, both secondary, and on the Codex's region record.
